p: Mohamed Amin Didi was born on 20 July 1910, the son of Athireegey Ahmed Dhoshimeynaa Kilegefaan and Roanugey Aishath Didi, and through his father a descendant of the Huraa dynasty. In 1920 he was sent to Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, to study at Saint Joseph's College in Colombo, and in 1928 he went to India for further studies at Aligarh Muslim University, returning to the Maldives a year later. He married Fathimath Saeed; their only child was a daughter, Annabeela Ameena Mohamed Amin.

In 1931 he was appointed to the Constituent Assembly convened by Sultan Muhammad Shamsuddeen III to draft the country's first written constitution. He went on to hold many posts: chief officer of customs, head of the post office, minister of trade, minister of education from 1933 to 1936 and from 1944 to 1952, minister of finance from 1942 to 1952 and minister of foreign affairs from 1944 to 1953. He sat in the first Maldivian parliament and was principal of Majeedhiyya School from 1946 to 1953.

He was appointed prime minister on 1 January 1947, at a time when the country was suffering widespread famine and exhausted resources after the Second World War. He led the first political party in the Maldives, the Rayyithunge Muthagaddim Party. His programme included the advancement of women and a ban on tobacco smoking. As prime minister he also wrote a booklet for foreigners, Ladies and Gentlemen: The Maldive Islands, on the life, culture and economy of the country.

According to a report in the newspaper Mihaaru, the revolt of 1953 was staged by Ibrahim Zaki, Mohamed Zaki and Ibrahim Nasir, who invited the vice-president, Ibrahim Muhammad Didi, to join; he agreed out of distaste for Amin's handling of state funds. A special assembly passed a vote of no confidence that handed all powers temporarily to Ibrahim Didi. Amin, in Sri Lanka, learned of events by letter but not of his removal. He returned by way of RAF Gan to Malé, was taken to Dhoonidhoo, where he was beaten by the army, and was then banished to Vihamanaafushi, where he died of health complications on 19 January 1954.

In September 2021 a member of parliament, Ibrahim Rasheed, lodged a case with the Office of the Ombudsperson for Transitional Justice seeking justice for his death and the overturning of his conviction as a traitor. The office's mandate expired on 19 November 2023.

notes: DATES: the article gives his presidency as 1 January to 21 August 1953 but says he left the premiership on 2 September 1953; I gave neither end date (the entry says overthrown in 1953).

The article says Ibrahim Didi 'ordered the Army to beat Amin' at Dhoonidhoo; I wrote that he was beaten by the army there, without naming who ordered it, as the sentence is from a single newspaper report.
The article is thin on his presidency itself; nothing is added on the republic beyond the entry.
